sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Significant correlations exist between the presence of intratumoral macrophages, tumor progression, and poor outcomes in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) with limited therapeutic options available for advanced-stage disease. Preclinical studies revealed that inhibition of myelomonocytic colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1) or its receptor (CSF1R) plus cytotoxic chemotherapy decreased primary tumor growth kinetics and pulmonary metastases by CD8+ T cell–dependent mechanisms. This translational study evaluated CSF1R inhibition combined with eribulin in metastatic TNBC and explored rational preclinical combination strategies with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade based on clinical immune correlate analyses.

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: A nonrandomized, open-label phase Ib/2 trial (NCT01596751) evaluated pexidartinib (PLX3397), a CSF1R inhibitor (CSF1Ri), plus eribulin mesylate in heavily pretreated individuals with metastatic TNBC. Clinical efficacy was assessed alongside peripheral blood correlates. Preclinical studies in transgenic mammary adenocarcinoma models examined biomarker-driven therapy combinations.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: The 12-week progression-free survival rate was 36% (95% confidence interval, 22.2%–58.4%), with 44.8% of patients achieving clinical benefit; a subset experienced disease control beyond 6 months. Patients with partial response or stable disease demonstrated increased baseline leukocyte activation, including enrichment of CD8+ and CD4+ memory T cells and increased PD-1 expression on CD4+ T cells. In preclinical studies, CSF1Ri expanded the therapeutic index of PD-1 blockade, yielding transient tumor regression in ∼60% of mice and a transient expansion of effector and resident memory T cells.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: These clinical and preclinical findings provide rationale for therapies to increase the therapeutic index of αPD-1 therapy by diminishing the presence of T cell–suppressive myelomonocytic cells to improve outcomes for patients with refractory disease.

boxed-text.p: We report results from a proof-of-concept translational study in patients with metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) with a therapy targeting the myelomonocytic colony-stimulating factor-1 (CSF1)/receptor (CSF1R) pathway combined with eribulin chemotherapy and identify correlate biomarkers indicating relief of various aspects of systemic immune suppression. Leveraging clinical biomarkers of response, preclinical transgenic mammary carcinoma modeling identified synergy with PD-1 blockade as a promising triple combination strategy with potential to benefit patients with refractory disease.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In the United States, an estimated 316,950 new cases of breast cancer were diagnosed, and ∼42,000 women died of breast cancer in 2025 (1). Although overall survival (OS) has improved for patients with early-stage breast cancer, only ∼30% of individuals diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer (mBC) survive beyond 5 years (2), with the poorest survival for patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Clinical trials have recently evaluated safety and efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) as either monotherapy or in combination with chemotherapy (CTX) in TNBC, leading to the approval of the PD-1 inhibitor pembrolizumab combined with CTX in patients with PD-L1–positive mTNBC and as neoadjuvant therapy for patients with high-risk early-stage TNBC irrespective of PD-L1 expression (3, 4). In the metastatic setting, less than 40% of patients with mTNBC are eligible for ICI therapy, and despite addition of newly approved antibody drug conjugates, the median survival after diagnosis of metastatic disease ranges from 1 to 2 years (5).

Poor outcomes for patients with mTNBC may be in part due to significant presence of T cell–suppressive myelomonocytic cells (monocytes and macrophages) in tumors (6–8). Accordingly, a colony-stimulating factor-1 (CSF1)-response gene expression signature predicts outcomes in 17% to 25% of breast cancers and is associated with reduced estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) expression (9) complimenting blood monocyte and tumor macrophage signatures as predictors of breast cancer clinical outcomes (8). In MMTV-PyMT (10) and C31-Tag (11) mouse models of mammary adenocarcinoma, tumors exhibit CSF1/CSF1 receptor (CSF1R)-regulated myelomonocytic infiltration and limited response to paclitaxel (PTX) CTX (6, 12) with no response to either PD-1 or PD-L1–targeted ICIs (13). Pexidartinib (PLX), a competitive ATP inhibitor with potent nmol/L specificity for CSF1R, cKIT, and FLT3 receptor tyrosine kinases (14), reduces the presence of intratumoral macrophages and, when combined with PTX or radiotherapy, slows tumor growth, and reduces pulmonary metastases via CD8+ T cell–dependent mechanisms in these mouse models, highlighting macrophages as key regulators of late-stage progression and T-cell suppression (6, 15).

Based on these preclinical findings, we hypothesized that inhibition of the CSF1/CSF1R signaling axis, in combination with eribulin CTX in patients with heavily pretreated mTNBC, would similarly lead to enhanced systemic antitumor immune responses and potentially improve clinical outcome. Prior early-phase clinical efforts with CSF1R blockade combined with CTX (gemcitabine, carboplatine, or PTX) reported on-target modulation of myelomonocytic cells albeit accompanied with frequent low-grade liver enzyme elevations and other class-specific toxicities that underscore the need to test alternative CTX partners (16). Herein, we report findings from a nonrandomized phase Ib/2 trial (NCT01596751) evaluating safety, tolerability, and 12-week progression-free survival (PFS) with PLX plus eribulin (a halichondrin analog FDA-approved for the treatment of mBC) in pretreated mBC, including a phase II mTNBC cohort. Enhanced systemic antitumor response features in some patients prompted preclinical evaluation of PD-1 blockade versus PD-L1 blockade in combination with PLX and PTX in MMTV-PyMT mice. The sequential three-drug combination with PD-1 blockade induced transient tumor regressions linked to effector and resident memory CD8+ T cell activation, compared with the combination with PD-L1 blockade. These data provide proof of concept that CSF1R inhibition plus microtubule poisons relieve aspects of immune suppression and synergize with selective ICIs, offering a strategy to enhance durable antitumor immunity.

sec.title: Patients, clinical trial design, and procedures
sec.p: This open-label, nonrandomized, phase Ib/2 study evaluated safety and efficacy of eribulin combined with PLX in patients with mBC. The primary objective of phase 1b was to determine maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of PLX with standard eribulin (1.4 mg/m2 intraveinously on days 1 and 8 of a 21-day cycle). The secondary objectives included safety and tolerability. Dose-limiting toxicities (DLT) included prolonged or febrile neutropenia, inability to receive both eribulin doses in cycle 1 due to toxicity, or >7-day delay in PLX dosing.

A 3 + 3 dose-escalation design evaluated PLX (400–1,000 mg daily, n = 28). The cohorts were observed ≥3 weeks before escalation; nontreatment-related withdrawals were replaced. The MTD was determined at 1,000 mg, and phase II opened.

The phase II study used a Simon two-stage design for 12-week PFS, referencing the EMBRACE trial (17). Stage 1 required ≥8 of 20 evaluable patients to achieve 12-week PFS to proceed; stage 2 targeted 51 evaluable patients, and 56 planned with 10% dropout. Due to myelosuppression in phase I, prophylactic growth factor support was mandated. The treatment included a 5-day PLX lead-in, with a 1- to 2-day break, followed by combination therapy with eribulin and PLX. After hepatic toxicity, PLX was reduced to 800 mg (400 mg twice daily) on a 5-day on/2-day off schedule. In one cohort, eribulin was administered every 15 days for neutropenia. The dose modifications followed standard practice, and corticosteroids were optional for antiemetic prophylaxis and symptom management. Tumor imaging occurred every 6 to 8 weeks. Laboratory tests were obtained before each eribulin infusion, with weekly liver function monitoring. Accrual stopped at 39 patients due to toxicity and limited efficacy.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: The phase Ib study enrolled patients ≥18 years of age with any subset of mBC, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status <2, life expectancy ≥12 weeks, and progressive after ≥1 prior CTX for advanced disease. HER2-positive patients required progression on prior trastuzumab; no other HER2-targeted therapies were available. The phase II study enrolled only mTNBC, defined as ER and PR <10%, with progression after ≥1 prior CTX. The key eligibility criteria included <grade I peripheral neuropathy, adequate bone marrow reserve (absolute neutrophil count >1,000/μL and platelets >100 K/μL), renal function [serum creatinine <1.5× upper limit of normal (ULN) or creatinine clearance >50 mL/minute], and hepatic function [alanine transaminase (AST), aspartate transaminase (ALT) <2.5× ULN; total bilirubin <1.5× ULN; and AST/ALT <5× ULN for liver metastases). The exclusion criteria included untreated heart failure, ejection fraction below institutional lower limit, or significant QT prolongation (>grade I, 480 ms). Stable treated brain metastases were allowed. A 2-week washout from prior therapy was required.

sec.title: Trial oversight
sec.p: This trial followed Good Clinical Practice and the Declaration of Helsinki. Institutional review boards (IRB) approved the protocol, and all patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: Funding and drug providers
sec.p: The clinical trial was funded through a Komen Promise award to H.S. Rugo, E.S. Hwang, and L.M. Coussens. Plexxikon, Inc. (now Daiichi Sankyo) provided PLX but played no role in study design and collection/analysis of data or article preparation. Eribulin was provided as standard of care. Syndax Pharmaceuticals provided αCSF1R mAb for preclinical studies.

sec.title: CSF-1 levels
sec.p: For the phase I trial, CSF1 levels were collected at C1D1, C1D2, and C2D1. For the phase II trial, CSF1 levels were collected at LI (5 to 7 days prior to the start of eribulin), C1D1, and C2D1.

sec.title: Leukocyte subtyping via flow cytometry
sec.p: Blood was collected at baseline for patients in phase I trial and at days −7/5 and 0/1 for patients in phase II trial.

sec.title: Phase I
sec.p: The phase I trial is a 3 + 3 dose-escalation design with three to six patients per cohort. Enrollment to successive cohorts is listed in Supplementary Table S1. If ≥2 DLTs occurred at level 0, one dose reduction (to level −1) was permitted.

sec.title: Phase II
sec.p: The primary efficacy endpoint was 12-week PFS (alive and progression-free 90 days after the start of the treatment). Efficacy was assessed in evaluable patients. Those without postbaseline tumor assessments were right censored on study day −1. Patients receiving subsequent anticancer therapy before an event were censored at the last tumor assessment prior to therapy. A Simon two-stage design was used, with a 3-month PFS rate of 57% (two-sided α = 0.05 and β = 0.20) and a null hypothesis of 39%. PFS was estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods with confidence intervals (CI). Objective response and clinical benefit rates were summarized with point estimates, interval estimates, and visualizations (e.g., Kaplan–Meier curves and Swimmer plots).

Safety data were summarized by adverse events (AEs, including severity, duration, and relationship to the study drug. Systemic immune biomarkers measured at baseline (C1D1), C2D1, and C4D1 were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model and repeated-measures ANOVA, with tumor response categories [partial response (PR)/stable disease (SD) or progressive disease (PD)] as a between-group factor. The optimal covariance structure was chosen using Bayesian information criteria. Contrast techniques tested preplanned comparisons, and false discovery rate correction was adjusted for multiple testing. Disease-free survival was compared between high- and low-level immune biomarker groups using Kaplan–Meier and log-rank tests.

sec.title: Phase II plasma and peripheral blood mononuclear cell analyses
sec.p: To determine concentrations of plasma proteins, the Luminex xMAP platform was used across time points, in which we first assigned to the lower limit the concentrations found below the lower limit of detection for a particular protein.

All other statistical analyses were performed using SAS (version 9.4), R (version 4.5.0), and Prism 9, as indicated in the Key Resource Table. Specific tests included Mann–Whitney (unpaired, nonparametric two-tailed), unpaired t test, one- and two-way ANOVA, and Wilcoxon rank-sum. In instances in which multiple comparisons were performed, the Bonferroni correction was used, unless otherwise specified. The number of animals per panel and specific tests are indicated in the respective figures. P values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant, with *, P < 0.05; **, P < 0.01; ***, P < 0.001; and ****, P < 0.0001, unless otherwise indicated in the figure.

sec.title: Human blood samples
sec.p: The human blood samples were collected in EDTA tubes. Plasma was separated from buffy coats by centrifugation (15-minute, 2,000 rpm, 4°C, brake off), transferred to cryovials, and then stored at −80°C. The buffy coats were incubated with 5× volume of 1× red blood cell (RBC) lysis buffer at room temperature (RT) for 5 minutes, protected from light, and then centrifuged (1,500 rpm, 5-minute, 4°C). The supernatant was removed, and the cell pellets were resuspended in freezing medium (RPMI, 10% DMSO, and 20% FBS). The samples were aliquoted, cooled at 1°C/minute in isopentanol-filled freezer cups overnight, and stored at −80°C.

sec.title: Animal husbandry and preclinical mouse studies
sec.p: FVB/n mice with the PyMT transgene under the control of the MMTV promoter were used (18). Eighty-day-old MMTV-PyMT female littermates were randomized by initial tumor volume and were fed PLX-formulated (40 mg/kg/day) or control chow until predetermined endpoints. At 85 days of age, the PLX-treated mice received PTX every 5 days by retroorbital intravenous injection (10 mg/kg in PBS). At 87 days, mice were treated with αPD-1, αPD-L1, or isotype control (1.0 mg/mouse initially and then 0.5 mg/mouse every 5 days by i.p. injection). Tumor burden was measured every 5 days using a caliper on sedated mice.

sec.title: Preclinical tumor growth kinetics
sec.p: Tumor growth was defined as the percent change in volume from the first day of combination treatment to the final day of measurement. The percent change was calculated as (final – initial)/initial × 100. For visualization, the percent change of tumor volume was categorized from decreasing to doubling divided into quartiles (decrease: <0%; slow: 0%–25%; medium: 25%–50%; fast: 50%–75%; very fast: 75%–100%; and more than double: >100%). The percent change in tumor volume was compared between groups using a pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum test with the P values adjusted for family-wise error rate (FWER) using the Hochberg method. For all violin plots, the medians are displayed as dashed line values, and dotted lines show interquartile ranges.

sec.title: Preclinical mouse studies—tissue harvest
sec.p: Tissues were flash-frozen, digested to single-cell suspensions, or fixed in formalin for paraffin embedding. All experiments adhered to NIH guidelines and were approved by the Oregon Health & Science University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

sec.title: Human
sec.p: Whole blood was collected in EDTA tubes and cryopreserved in FBS 10% DMSO following written informed consent and supervision by the IRB. Cryopreserved samples were thawed in 30 mL of prewarmed RPMI with 2% FBS and 0.5 mmol/L of EDTA and centrifuged for 5 minutes at 400 g. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) were isolated by RBC lysis, washed twice in PBS with 2% FBS/0.5 mmol/L of EDTA, and incubated with FcR blocking solution prior to staining with indicated antibodies for immunophenotyping. Multiparametric flow cytometry was performed on a BD LSRFortessa using FACSDiva Software, and analyses were conducted in FlowJo. The frequencies within the CD45+ compartment were reported due to variability in cryopreserved PBMC volumes. Additional analyses were performed with R.

sec.title: Murine
sec.p: The single-cell suspensions were generated from tumors, draining lymph nodes (dLN), and lungs of cardiac-perfused mice by mechanical dissociation and 30-minute digestion with DNase I (50 U/mL) and collagenase A (2.0 mg/mL for tumors and 1.0 mg/mL for dLNs and lungs) in serum-free DMEM at 37°C. Blood was collected via retroorbital sinus and lysed with BD PharmLyse. Cells were incubated at 4°C with rat antimouse FcR blocking solution (1:500) and Live/Dead Aqua stain (1:800), stained with fluorophore-conjugated antimouse antibodies in PBS with 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA) and 2.0 mmol/L of EDTA, fixed with BD Cytofix, and acquired on a BD LSRFortessa using FACSDiva software. Data were analyzed in FlowJo. The PBMCs were cryopreserved with the proportions of cells reported as the percent of CD45+.

sec.title: Luminex
sec.p: The Luminex xMAP Multi-Analyte Profiling platform quantified multiple proteins in the same plasma sample of each patient across time points according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue staining and analysis
Histopathology
sec.p: Tissue samples from PBS cardiac-perfused mice were fixed in 10% formalin, dehydrated, and embedded in paraffin. Histopathologic analysis was performed on 5-μm sections of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues from 95- or 105-day-old MMTV-PyMT mice. The sections were baked at 60°C, deparaffinized, rehydrated, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin. Tumor grade was assessed and staged based on a previously described scheme (6), from “precancerous” hyperplasia and adenoma to “early carcinoma” with stromal invasion and finally “late-stage carcinoma” with high mitotic index. Metastatic burden was determined by counting metastatic foci (>5 cells) in 100-μm spaced sections of FFPE lung tissue, with data from >10 mice/group.

sec.title: Tissue preparation
sec.p: Tissues were fixed with 10% neutral-buffered formalin, dehydrated in ethanol, and paraffin-embedded using standard protocols. Briefly, tissue sections were deparaffinized and subjected to antigen retrieval for 20 minutes via steam heating in Citra solution or proteinase K, followed by endogenous peroxidase blockade at RT for 10 minutes in Dako Dual Endogenous Enzyme Block. The sections were incubated for 10 minutes at RT with blocking buffer containing 5% goat serum and 2.5% BSA.

sec.title: Standard immunohistochemistry
sec.p: Standard immunohistochemistry (IHC) on mouse tissues was performed by incubating primary antibodies for 1 hour at RT: rat anti-BrdU (1:2,000) and rat antimouse cleaved caspase 3 (1:200). The sections were incubated with biotinylated secondary antibodies (1:500), followed by horseradish peroxidase–conjugated avidin complex (ABC Elite) for 30 minutes and development with Fast 3,3-diaminobenzidine. The sections were counterstained with methyl green, dehydrated, mounted with Cytoseal 60, coverslipped with Signature Series Cover Glass, and digitally scanned at 20× using an Aperio ImageScope. Image visualization and quantification of single-cell positive signal (the name of the algorithm used) were performed using ImageScope Software (Leica Biosystems). Quantification was conducted either manually (five high-powered fields per mouse, averaged) or automatically [entire region of interest (ROI) analyzed and normalized to total area].

sec.title: Multiplexed IHC
sec.p: Multiplex IHC (mIHC) on mouse tissue sections was performed as previously described (19, 20). Briefly, 5-μm sections on Tanner slides were incubated with primary antibodies for 30 to 60 minutes at RT or overnight at 4°C; antibody and staining conditions are listed in the Key Resources Table. The slides were scanned at 20× using an Aperio AT2 scanner. After completion of all markers, ROIs were selected in Aperio ImageScope, and images were coregistered in MATLAB R2018b using the SURF algorithm (Computer Vision Toolbox). Color deconvolution, segmentation, and cell quantification were performed using FIJI Is Just ImageJ (FIJI); ref. 21) and CellProfiler v3.5.1 (22). CellProfiler outputs were analyzed in FCS Express 7 Image Cytometry RUO (De Novo Software) with hierarchical gating to classify NK cells (PANCK− CD3− KLRBC1+), CD3+ T cells (PANCK− CD3+), and neoplastic cells (PANCK+).

sec.title: Lung metastatic foci area and shape descriptors
sec.p: Metastatic foci were identified based on the structure after hematoxylin staining. The outlines of metastatic foci were traced in ImageJ software. The area of the outline (indicating the foci area) was calculated using ImageJ software. The FIJI shape descriptor “circularity” was used to assess the level of “dispersedness” or “solidness” of a metastatic focus. The formula for circularity is as follows:4π × [Area][Perimeter]2
The values approaching “1” represent perfect circles. The values approaching “0” indicate increasingly elongated polygons.

sec.title: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
sec.p: Plasma protein levels of secreted cytokines and chemokines IFNγ, CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11 levels were measured using precoated enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) plates according to the manufacturer’s instructions. ELISA kits included mouse IFNγ kit, mouse CXCL9 kit, mouse CXCL10 kit, and mouse CXCL11 kit.

sec.title: RNA isolation
sec.p: For the nCounter Mouse PanCancer IO360 NanoString panel, 10 to 20 mg of snap-frozen tumors were crushed in liquid nitrogen, and RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Micro Kit. cDNA was synthesized using SuperScript VILO, and 50 ng was used for multiplex target enrichment. The samples were hybridized with NanoString probes for 17 hours at 65°C and loaded into an nCounter SPRINT cartridge.

sec.title: NanoString normalization and pathway analysis
sec.p: Quality control of NanoString data was performed with nSolver Analysis Software version 4.0.70. Housekeeping gene stability and correlation were assessed using the geNorm and PairwiseV functions from the ctlGene package in R. Out of 20 genes included in the NanoString ImmuneOncology 360 panel, 10 genes were deemed fit for data normalization of the raw data: Sdha, Tbc1d10b, G6pdx, Dnajc14, Sf3a1, Abcf1, Ercc3, Pum1, Polr2a, and Nrde2. All selected genes had expression above NanoString limit of detection (LOD) with data normalized (30). The data were normalized following Bhattacharya and colleagues (23), before unwanted technical variance was estimated with RUVg from the RUVseq package (24), using only the subset of housekeeping genes selected with geNorm and PairwiseV. Raw counts were transformed using the varianceStabilizing transformation (VST) function from the DEseq2 package, and factors of unwanted variance estimated by RUVg were removed with removeBatchEffect from the Limma package. Annotations of selected signaling pathways and functions were used to evaluate intergroup variation. Single-sample enrichment scores were computed using gsva (GSVA package) with VST scaled count data as input. Heatmaps were generated using Pheatmap after mean-centering VST scaled count data per gene.

sec.title: TCRβ deep sequencing of tumor and blood
sec.p: Genomic DNA was isolated from PBMCs, tumor, and lung single-cell suspensions using the DNeasy Mini Kit. Approximately 600 ng (PBMCs) and 1,500 ng (tumor and lung) of DNA were used for TCRβ PCR as previously described (25). Briefly, TCRβ was amplified by the two-stage multiplex PCR with barcoding, pooled equally, and prepared for deep sequencing. The libraries were quantified by real-time PCR (StepOne Real-Time Workstation) after 2200 TapeStation profiling and sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 500 (2 × 150, Midoutput 300; ∼160 million clusters/run). The reads were quality-checked, merged using PEAR (26) per (25), and CDR3 sequences were extracted using MiXCR (27). Clonotype counts were normalized for PCR bias (28) and used to calculate diversity and overlap metrics (clonal frequency, clonality, Shannon diversity, and Jaccard index) as in (25). Public clonotypes were tracked using Immunarch R package version 0.9.1 (29).

sec.title: RNA isolation
sec.p: For the nCounter Mouse PanCancer IO360 NanoString panel, 10 to 20 mg of snap-frozen tumors were crushed in liquid nitrogen, and RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Micro Kit. cDNA was synthesized using SuperScript VILO, and 50 ng was used for multiplex target enrichment. The samples were hybridized with NanoString probes for 17 hours at 65°C and loaded into an nCounter SPRINT cartridge.

sec.title: Safety, tolerability, 12-week PFS, and response following PLX plus eribulin
sec.p: To address the hypothesis that CSF1/CSF1R pathway inhibition would improve clinical response to standard-of-care CTX, we conducted a nonrandomized phase Ib/2 trial (NCT01596751) with eribulin (17) combined with PLX (31), FDA-approved for the treatment of tenosynovial giant cell tumors (32). Patients were enrolled at the University of California San Francisco, Vanderbilt, and Duke universities (Fig. 1A). The phase Ib study enrolled patients from July 24, 2011 to December 12, 2014, followed by phase II enrollment from January 28, 2015 to March 7, 2017. Patient demographics and disease characteristics are summarized in Supplementary Table S1, and representativeness or participants in Supplementary Table S2. Twenty-eight patients were accrued, and the MTD for PLX was determined to be 1,000 mg (Supplementary Tables S3 and S4). Circulating CSF1 levels, a known pharmacodynamic indicator of CSF1R inhibition, were monitored for changes during dose escalation with specific doses of PLX (Supplementary Fig. S1A). The complete list of serious AEs for phase Ib is outlined in Supplementary Table S5; the primary DLTs were neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, rash, and elevation in liver enzymes.

caption.p: Trial design and treatment response. A, Study design for phase Ib and phase II. P.O., orally. B, Sample collection and time points for those enrolled on phase II. C, Kaplan–Meier curve of PFS for the phase II cohort. D, Swimmer plot showing best response across the phase II cohort, with each row reflecting an individual patient.

sec.p: The phase II portion of the trial included patients with pretreated mTNBC; 39 patients were enrolled (Supplementary Table S6); enrollment was subsequently discontinued because of toxicity. Study design and treatment schedule are presented in Fig. 1B. The changes in dose and schedule were implemented in response to observed toxicities. Seventeen patients received 1,000 mg of PLX, which was then reduced to 800 mg for the subsequent 22 patients. In the 35 patients evaluable for efficacy, 12-week PFS was 36% (95% CI, 22.2%–58.4%). The median PFS was 42 days (95% CI, 40–116 days), calculated from the initiation of combination therapy with a wide range from 7 to 233 days, with two patients demonstrating prolonged disease control beyond 180 days (Fig. 1C). Clinical benefit, defined as at least one scan without progression, was observed in 13 patients; SD in nine (26%), PR in four (11.4%), whereas 19 (55.2%) experienced PD (Fig. 1D). Three patients stopped therapy early because of toxicity without imaging. Common toxicities (Supplementary Table S7) included neutropenia, fatigue, nausea, dyspnea, rash, AST/ALT elevation, and mucositis/pharyngitis (26%; one grade III). Grade ≥III events included febrile neutropenia, AST/ALT elevation, and one case of drug-induced liver injury with vanishing bile duct syndrome (C2). Despite dose/schedule modifications, enrollment was discontinued because of intolerable toxicity.

sec.title: PLX plus eribulin activates peripheral antitumoral leukocyte responses
sec.p: Correlative studies of serial blood from 39 patients with mTNBC (phase II) examined soluble mediators and peripheral immune cells (secondary endpoints; Fig. 2; Supplementary Fig. S2A–S2V). Based on phase I PLX data (16) and CSF1’s role in monocyte maturation and circulating CSF1 levels (33), monotherapy rapidly reduced CD14dimCD16hi nonclassical monocytes in 95% of evaluable patients at C1D1 (P < 0.001), confirming target engagement. In combination with eribulin, nonclassical monocytes remained similar to the initial proportions of 94% at C2D1 and 88% at C4D1 (Fig. 2A; Supplementary Fig. S2B and S2E). Plasma CSF1 varied across patients, and CCL2 increased significantly with PLX monotherapy (Fig. 2B and C). Additional soluble indicators of leukocyte activation—including IFNγ, CXCL10, CXCL11, TNFRSF8, TNFRSF1B, CCL22, CCL24, IL15, and IL2RA—increased significantly following the addition of eribulin, indicating systemic modulation of leukocyte trafficking and effector signaling (Fig. 2D; Supplementary Fig. S2A).

sec.p: To further evaluate the therapeutic effect on circulating leukocytes, we utilized multiparametric flow cytometry (Supplementary Fig. S2B–S2R) and revealed a significant decrease in dendritic cell (DC) subsets following PLX monotherapy (Supplementary Fig. S2F) as anticipated based on PLX suppression of Flt3. Combination treatment, however, led to significantly increased presence of natural killer (NK) cells between C1D1 and C2D1 (Fig. 2E; Supplementary Fig. S2F and S2G). Although overall T cell frequencies remained more or less stable throughout cycles (Supplementary Fig. S2G), we sought to better define the effect of combination therapy on T cell activation and effector status at each cycle (Fig. 2F–H; Supplementary Fig. S2C and S2G–S2L). Following combination therapy, increased frequencies of CD4+ and CD8+ T effector memory (EM) and T central memory (CM) cells (Fig. 2F) with evidence of enhanced proliferation (Ki67 positivity) were apparent (Fig. 2G and H). Increased proliferative trends were also observed in terminally differentiated effector memory T cells (TEMRA), indicating their activated following combination therapy (Supplementary Fig. S2K and S2L).

Based on increased expression of IFNγ and enhanced proliferation of select T cell subsets, we hypothesized that the expression of PD-L1 and/or PD-1 might also be affected by therapy and potentially correlate with clinical responses. To evaluate this, we assessed PD-L1 and PD-1 expression in paired CD45+ PBMCs at LI, C1D1, and C2D1. PD-L1 expression in PBMCs and CD45− cells revealed marked interindividual heterogeneity, with no statistically significant net change at the cohort level with both increases and decreases observed across time points. PBMCs from 26% of patients exhibited increased PD-L1 expression by >10% at C1D1 as compared with LI (P < 0.001) and 50% of patients with increased PD-L1 >10% at C2D1 (P < 0.0003; Fig. 2I; Supplementary Fig. S2M). PD-L1 expression trends similarly increased in CD45− PBMCs (presumably circulating tumor cells, plasma cells, erythroid precursors, and blasts) from C1D1 to C2D1 (Supplementary Fig. S2M). The main contributors to CD45+ PD-L1 changes were classic, intermediate, and nonclassical monocytes and cDC1 subsets, as shown by clinical response (Supplementary Fig. S2N and S2O). Similarly, PD-1 expression on T cell subsets—reflecting enhanced antigen presentation—revealed 41% of patients with >10% increase in CD4+ T cells at C1D1 (P < 0.002) versus LI, rising to 64% by C2D1 (P < 0.002), including regulatrory T (TREG) cells (Supplementary Fig. S2P). On CD8+ T cells, 36% of patients had >10% PD-1 increase at C2D1 (P < 0.04; Supplementary Fig. S2Q). Notably, CD4+ T cell PD-1 expression was higher in patients with SD or PR after combination therapy (Fig. 2J), indicating enhanced T cell activation linked to clinical benefit. Correspondingly, plasma CXCL9, TNFRSF8, and TLSP increased and stratified patients by response (Supplementary Fig. S2R), indicating coordinated systemic activation of leukocyte trafficking, effector programs, and tissue repair pathways underlying therapeutic effects.

To assess whether peripheral leukocyte composition or state predicted SD/PR, we found that higher than median myeloid DC (mDC) frequencies during the first cycles (LI-C2D1) associated with improved survival (Supplementary Fig. S2S and S2T). Similarly, increased PD-L1 expression on total monocytes during combination therapy (C1D1–C2D1, Supplementary Fig. S2U and S2V) correlated with better outcomes. Together, increased leukocyte trafficking and higher frequencies of proliferating TEM and CM cells in PBMCs indicated systemic leukocyte activation. These findings support the notion that peripheral biomarkers are useful to monitor immune responses for clinically relevant outcomes and may reflect, at least partially, contextual changes in intratumoral leukocytes, reflecting relief of systemic immune suppression.

sec.title: CSF1R inhibition/PTX therapy leads to increased expression of PD-1 and PD-L1 in murine mammary tumors, metastatic lungs, and peripheral blood leukocytes
sec.p: Based on the clinical correlates of response to PLX and eribulin, we hypothesized that similar biomarkers of response and resistance would be observed in transgenic mammary tumor models that could inform future combination strategies. We, therefore, examined the MMTV-PyMT mammary carcinoma model (18), assessing the murine correlates of immune activation identified in patients (e.g., IFNγ, CXCL-9, -10, and -11) in the circulating blood of mice following PTX/CSF1R blockade (2× therapy) at late stage (105 days of age, d105) using a blocking αCSF1R mAb. Optimal macrophage diminution occurred 3 days after treatment and persisted up to 7 days (Supplementary Fig. S3A), defining the treatment schema (Fig. 3A) and enabling assessment of intratumoral MHCIIhigh (Supplementary Fig. S3B) and MHCIIlow (Supplementary Fig. S3C) macrophages. Consistent with the clinical findings, plasma IFNγ, CXCL-9, -10, and -11 were significantly elevated with combination therapy, showing ≥2-fold increases versus monotherapies (Fig. 3B). Given the role of IFNγ in leukocyte activation and PD-L1 induction, we analyzed immune composition and PD-L1/PD-1 expression in vehicle-, PTX-, or PTX/PLX-treated mice (2× therapy) across primary tumors, metastatic lungs, and blood (Fig. 3C). Intratumorally, PTX increased TAMs and neutrophils, whereas 2× therapy reduced TAMs (Fig. 3D; Supplementary Fig. S3D). CD11b+ and CD103+ DCs and Ly6C+ monocytes expanded, with reduced neutrophils and B cells and no change in overall CD3+ lymphocytes with 2× therapy. PD-L1 expression increased mainly in myeloid cells, particularly MHCIIhi TAMs, monocytes, and DCs after PTX, and on residual TAMs and monocytes after 2× therapy; PD-1 increased in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells with 2× therapy (Fig. 3D).

sec.p: In metastatic lungs, interstitial and alveolar macrophages decreased, whereas CD11b+ DCs, neutrophils, CD8+, and CD4−CD8− T cells increased after PTX and 2× therapy (Fig. 3E; Supplementary Fig. S3E). PD-L1 was broadly upregulated on myeloid subsets, predominantly macrophages and monocytes, with concomitant PD-1 induction on CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. In blood, DCs and CD8+ T cells increased following 2× therapy, paralleling human phase II samples (Fig. 3F; Supplementary Fig. S3F); PD-L1 induction was confined to DCs and Ly6C+ monocytes, with increased PD-1 on T cells. Collectively, murine data recapitulated human blood biomarkers and revealed that one mechanism of PTX resistance is associated with PD-L1 induction on DCs, monocytes, and tumor macrophages.

sec.title: Transient primary tumor regression with PTX/CSF1R inhibition/PD-1 blockade but not with PD-L1 combination
sec.p: We investigated whether CSF1R inhibition alleviated T cell dysfunction and promoted proliferative memory T cell responses following ICI therapy. MMTV-PyMT mice were treated with monotherapy, double (2×), or triple (3×) drug combinations (PLX/PTX + αPD-1 or αPD-L1) and assessed primary tumor burden, growth kinetics, immune contexture, and incidence and features of pulmonary metastases (Fig. 4A; Supplementary Fig. S4). At Institutional Animal Care andUse Committee (IACUC) endpoints, tumors from all PLX-containing combinations showed significantly reduced volumes (Fig. 4A). Prospective growth analyses revealed significant differences among groups (Supplementary Fig. S4A and S4B), with PTX/PLX/αPD-1 (3×-αPD-1) exhibiting the lowest growth curve (slope = 66.39 vs. 125.1 for 2×), followed by PTX/PLX/αPD-L1 (slope = 93.7). Notably, two kinetic patterns emerged in the 3×-αPD-1 group, including transient tumor regression (Fig. 4B). Tumor growth rates from day 8 to day 18 revealed that 2× therapy slowed growth in 100% of mice versus controls or PTX alone (P < 0.0001), similar to αPD-1/PTX (P < 0.001). Importantly, 3× αPD-1 induced regression in 64% of mice (3×R), evident by day 10, with regression occurring across all mammary glands (Supplementary Fig. S4C), whereas mice with nonregressing mammary tumors (3×NR) lacked this phenotype. Briefly, 54% of the PTX/αPD-L1 cohort and 14% of the 3×-αPD-L1 cohort showed modest evidence of primary tumor regression; however, the extent of regression was <30% change from day 8 (Supplementary Fig. S4C). Depletion studies demonstrated that regression was largely CD8+ T cell–dependent between days 10 and 15, with CD4+ T cell and NK cell depletion indicating modest degree of tumor control (Supplementary Fig. S4D–S4F).

sec.p: Histopathologic analyses revealed lower tumor grades with increased preinvasive and early carcinoma regions in 3×-αPD-1-R tumors (Supplementary Fig. S4G and S4H). Circulating PyMT gene expression, reflecting circulating tumor cells, was lowest in 3×-αPD-1 mice (Supplementary Fig. S4I). Pulmonary metastases are primarily driven by CSF1R signaling in intratumoral TAMs (34), and as previously reported for 2× therapy (6) they remained low in all PLX-treated groups; low abundance of both macro- and micrometastatic foci was maintained in all treatment groups receiving PLX (Supplementary Fig. S4J–S4L). However, 3×-αPD-1-R mice exhibited significantly fewer circular metastatic foci (Supplementary Fig. S4M), associated with increased CD3−KLRB1c+ NK cells and CD3+ T cells by mIHC (Supplementary Fig. S4N and S4O), indicating enhanced immune infiltration and tumor margin disruption. The Spearman correlation analyses between circularity and immune cell infiltration revealed a weak but statistically significant relationship; circularity was inversely associated with proportions of T (r = −0.2341 and P < 0.0001) and NK cells (r = −0.1936, P < 0.0001; Supplementary Fig. S4P and S4Q). Metastatic circularity reflects various parameters, including tumor cell invasiveness, stromal composition, extracellular matrix constraints, vascular architecture, and immune infiltrate. The T cells and NK cells act mainly via cytotoxicity and cytokine signaling rather than direct modulation of lesion geometry; therefore, effects on circularity are likely secondary, explaining the Spearman test results. Collectively, these findings indicate that PD-1, but not PD-L1 blockade following CSF1R inhibition plus CTX, induces systemic and local antitumor immune features and primary tumor regression.

sec.title: Effect on immune contexture
sec.p: To elucidate mechanistic and/or contextual differences between 3×-αPD-1 and 3×-αPD-L1 responses, we first assessed intratumoral leukocyte subsets by CD45+ cell frequency across treatment groups (Fig. 4C; Supplementary Fig. S4R–S4Y). PLX-containing therapies reduced TAM presence in all groups (Fig. 4C; Supplementary Fig. S4S and S4T). 3×-αPD-1-R tumors contained significantly higher density of CD103+ DCs, linked to Th1 responses as compared with 3×-αPD-L1; CD11b+ DCs were more abundant in 3×-αPD-1-R versus 3×-αPD-1NR (Fig. 4D and E). To investigate whether density differences were linked to DC activation, we performed transcriptomic analysis via NanoString to assess Ag presentation indicators (Fig. 4F). Both 3×-αPD-1 and 3×-αPD-L1 therapies increased CD103+ cDC enrichment and tumor inflammation signatures (e.g., CD40, CXCL11, CXCL10, and CXCL9) known to correlate with ICI benefit [Fig. 4F (bottom heatmap)]. At the protein level, 3×-αPD-1-R correlated with significant upregulation of costimulatory molecules (CD86 and IL12) and MHCII on CD103+ cDCs compared with other groups (Fig. 4G–I; Supplementary Fig. S4Z). These findings indicate that tumor regression in 3×-αPD-1-R is likely related to DC activation, select cytokine secretion, and enhanced recruitment/activation of memory T cells, consistent with other studies (35).

sec.title: T resident memory cell expansion following CSF1R inhibition/PTX/αPD-1 therapy
sec.p: We next evaluated whether parameters of DC activation affected T cell densities or induction of memory T cell phenotypes; the 3×-αPD-L1 group increased CD3+ T cells as a proportion of CD45+ cells (Supplementary Fig. S5A), whereas CD8+ and CD4+ T cell densities (as a percentage of CD3+ cells) did not vary across groups (Supplementary Fig. S5B and S5C). Using multiparametric flow cytometry, we evaluated memory T cell populations, including CD8+ TCM, TEM, and TRM cells, and their proliferative (Ki67+) and cytotoxic (granzyme B+) properties (Fig. 5A–I). CD8+ TCM cell proportions were unchanged, whereas proliferation and granzyme B expression were significantly elevated in both 3×-αPD-1-R and 3×-αPD-L1 groups compared with controls (Fig. 5A–C). CD8+ TEM density remained stable, whereas their proliferation and granzyme B levels were higher in both 3×-αPD-1-R and 3×-αPD-L1 (Fig. 5D–F). Notably, 3×-αPD-1-R tumors revealed a significant increase in CD8+ TRM cells, correlating with enhanced proliferation and cytotoxicity (Fig. 5H and I).

sec.p: The density and granzyme B–positive CD8+ TSCM cells were unchanged across treatments (Supplementary Fig. S5D–S5F), whereas Ki67+ TSCM cells were significantly expanded in 3×-αPD-1-R tumors (Fig. 5E). About CD4+ T cells, overall CD4+ TCM were increased following PTX with no significant functional difference further observed across combination treatments (Fig. 5H and I). 3×-αPD-L1 significantly increased CD4+ TEM, which also showed enhanced proliferation and granzyme B expression (Supplementary Fig. S5J–S5L). PTX and PTX/PLX increased CD4+ TRM density, retaining proliferative and cytotoxic activity, which was lost in αPD-L1 but preserved with αPD-1 (Supplementary Fig. S5M and S5O). These results indicate that CD4+ effector cells play a lesser, albeit important role in the antitumor response.

To investigate whether T cell changes were Ag-specific or due to inflammatory cytokine signaling, we harvested tumors at day 95 (d95) and found TRM and TEM expansion and cytotoxicity at tumor regression onset in 3×-αPD-1 mice (Supplementary Fig. S5P–S5W). To examine Ag-specific activation, we used MMTV-PyMT/eGFP (Nr4a1) reporter mice (Supplementary Fig. S5V) expressing eGFP regulated by the Nur77 (NR4A1) promoter (36). Nur77 is a highly conserved orphan nuclear receptor and immediate-early gene whose expression is rapidly upregulated following TCR activation by Ag in murine T cells and human thymocytes. GFP is upregulated by strong Ag receptor stimulation through NR4A1, and unlike CD69, the early marker of T cell activation, is not induced by inflammatory stimuli. This study revealed stronger eGFP signals (gMFI) in 3×-αPD-1-R tumors compared with other treatments (Supplementary Fig. S5W) with twice the density of CD8+ TRM cells versus PTX, with increased proliferation and cytotoxicity (Fig. 5G–J), correlating with tumor regression.

sec.title: Differential TCR repertoires following CSF1R inhibition/PTX/αPD-1 versus αPD-L1 combinations
sec.p: We hypothesized that T cell contexture data and CD8+ TRM expansion following Ag-TCR engagement indicated clonal T cell expansion. Accordingly, deep sequencing of the TCRβ CDR3 region on primary tumors, lungs, and blood from cardiac-perfused tumor-bearing mice at end-stage (d105) after mono and combination therapies was performed (Fig. 4A). Repertoire diversity was assessed using clonal index, Shannon entropy, clonal homeostasis, and identification of shared clones across tissues and treatments. The clonal index was significantly increased in 3×-αPD-1-R samples, largely driven by the top five clones (Fig. 6A–C). Hyperexpanded clones were most frequent in PLX- and 3×-αPD-1-R groups (Fig. 6D), indicating that CSF1R inhibition alleviated T cell suppression synergistically with αPD-1, but not αPD-L1, blockade.

sec.p: Comparison of the top 100 clones revealed greater overlap between 3×-αPD-1-R and NR tumors than with αPD-L1 groups (Fig. 6E; Supplementary Fig. S6A). Clonotype tracking of the top 50 clones revealed that shared clones between 3×-αPD-1-R and -NR expanded exclusively in 3×-αPD-1-R (up to four-fold; Fig. 6F). In contrast, 3×-αPD-L1 exhibited a more diverse repertoire with minimal overlap and limited expansion, with overlapping clones also present in 3×-αPD-1-R (Fig. 6G). No significant differences in clonality or Shannon entropy were observed in metastatic lungs across triple therapies (Supplementary Fig. S6B–S6D); however, large clones predominated in 3×-αPD-L1, whereas medium clones were enriched in 3×-αPD-1-R and -NR (Supplementary Fig. S6D and S6E).

Clonotype tracking identified tumor-associated clones shared with metastatic lungs and circulating blood (Fig. 6H–J; Supplementary Fig. S6G) in which two clonotypes (V132 J2-5 CASGDAGDQDTQYF and V133 J2-4 CASSDSSQNTLYF) expanded in both (Fig. 6H and I), consistent with 3×-αPD-1–mediated expansion during transient tumor regression and relief of systemic immune suppression. In contrast, 3×-αPD-L1 tumors revealed the expansion of three intratumoral clones without dissemination (Fig. 6J; Supplementary Fig. S6H) and with substantial heterogeneity across individual 3×-αPD-L1 specimens indicating that the magnitude of tumor-specific clonal expansion was more limited and variable. These observations support the interpretation that 3×-αPD-1 therapy drives more robust and focused clonal expansion, consistent with its higher response rate, while highlighting that clonal metrics must be interpreted cautiously in the context of differences in infiltrate size and diversity. Despite seeing four mice in the 3×-αPD-L1 cohort showing primary tumor regression, only one could be evaluated for TCR clonality metrics which did not reveal differences between samples from similarly treated specimens, nor similarities with 3×-αPD-1–regressing tumors.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Extensive clinical and preclinical evidence supports targeting CSF1R+ myelomonocytic cells in combination with CTX or ICIs due to their role in tumor progression (37), motivating clinical development of CSF1/CSF1R-modulating therapies (38). However, CSF1R inhibition has shown limited monotherapy efficacy in advanced cancers (39, 40), except in tenosynovial giant cell tumors in which PLX is FDA-approved (41) and for graft versus host disease in which the highly specific anti-CSF1R mAb axatilimab is FDA-approved (42, 43).

In this study, we demonstrate biological activity of CSF1R inhibition combined with CTX in a nonrandomized phase Ib/2 mTNBC study (NCT01596751). Phase I study defined the MTD of PLX plus eribulin, whereas phase II study assessed 12-week PFS, ORR, DOR, and peripheral immune biomarkers. Although conducted prior to the approval of pembrolizumab–CTX (3) and sacituzumab govitecan (44), the trial revealed DLTs, including hepatotoxicity, consistent with prior reports for CSF1R inhibitors (16) limiting efficacy evaluation. The 12-week PFS was 36% with a short median PFS (42 days) but broad range (up to 233 days), indicating benefit in a subset. Despite limited feasibility, correlative and preclinical analyses provided mechanistic insight into CSF1/CSF1R targeting in mTNBC.

CSF1R blockade increased circulating CSF1 in a dose-dependent manner (Supplementary Fig. S1A), consistent with compensatory feedback observed in mice and humans (31, 45). Sustained CSF1 elevation, increased CCL2, and depletion of CD14dimCD16hi monocytes confirmed on-target PLX activity (Fig. 2A and B; Supplementary Fig. S2F) and align with CSF1R-regulated monocyte development (33). Based on preclinical PLX + PTX studies showing CD103+ DC- and CD8+ T cell–dependent tumor control (6, 12, 46, 47), we hypothesized immune activation clinically. Indeed, increased IL12A, cDC1s, CD4+/CD8+ TCM and TEM, and NK cells were observed, supporting a model in which CSF1R inhibition plus CTX promotes cDC1 maturation and IL12-driven (re)priming of PD-1+ T cells, likely resulting from reduced levels of macrophage IL10 (12). Although PFS was not extended, these findings indicate systemic immune reprogramming that may sensitize tumors to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade and underscore the value of peripheral immune monitoring.

Functionally, triple-combination studies in MMTV-PyMT mice revealed that only 3×-αPD-1 induced primary tumor regression, associated with Ag-specific CD8+ TRM activation, proliferation, and cytotoxicity. In contrast, 3×αPD-L1 expanded DCs and enhanced CD4+ TEM cytotoxicity and CD8+ TCM granzyme B expression without clonal expansion, likely indicating bystander T cell activation and increased repertoire diversity. The absence of CD4+ Ag specificity or depletion studies limited the attribution of tumor control in this group.

Several strategies to combine ICI/CTX in TNBC have been reported with promising results (48); however, a considerable obstacle remains in identifying the best candidates for these combinations. Clinically, reliance on PD-L1 expression for patient stratification is challenged by cellular heterogeneity (49, 50). Importantly, heterogeneous PD-L1 patterns contrast with increased PD-1 expression we observed from C1D1 to C2D1, associated with clinical benefit. This dissociation implies that adaptive immune checkpoint engagement may be driven primarily by PD-1 upregulation on immune cells rather than by uniform PD-L1 induction in circulating compartments, thereby supporting the biological rationale for therapeutic αPD-1 blockade to enhance antitumor immunity. Interestingly, PFS benefit has been observed in clinical settings combining αPD-L1 and CTX regardless of PD-L1 expression status (51) raising the intriguing possibility that responses might be further improved by CSF1R blockade when tumors express PD-L1 on neoplastic cells, as opposed to myelomonocytic lineages.

Consistent with robust CD8+ T cell expansion and tumor regression in 3×-αPD-1–treated mice, we conclude that CSF1R inhibition plus CTX and PD-1 blockade relieves systemic immune suppression and promotes intratumoral CD8+ TRM (re)priming. CD8+ TRM cells are associated with improved prognosis (52–55), and their clonal expansion in 3×R-αPD-1 cohorts aligns with evidence linking TRM density to survival and immune equilibrium (55, 56). These findings complement clinical advances with pembrolizumab plus CTX in early and mTNBC and support CSF1R blockade as an immunomodulatory adjunct to enhance the therapeutic index for PD-1/PD-L1 blockade and further improve outcome as supported by our and other studies (57, 58).

Lack of efficacy of PLX with αPD-L1 in pancreatic cancer has been attributed to DC depletion (39) due in part to PLX inhibition of FLT3 (IC50 of 160 nmol/L vs. 13 nmol/L toward CSF1R; ref. 59). We observed reduction of mDCs with monotherapy in accordance with these studies, whereas PLX + eribulin increased cDC1s indicating that a synergistic effect after CTX enhanced tumor neoantigen release likely via immunogenic cell death and positively balances leukocyte recruitment and activation. Despite transient regression in 3×-αPD-1–treated mice, durability was limited, as only a fraction of regressors maintained a low tumor burden to IACUC endpoint. Although our preclinical studies do not fully model chemoresistant TNBC, our approach supports early or priming-based deployment of myeloid modulation to enhance T cell–mediated immunity.

Overall, despite clinical toxicity, our data indicate that CSF1R inhibition plus CTX synergistically activates antitumoral immunity, which can be further enhanced by PD-1 blockade. Durable benefit will likely require optimized drug sequencing, identification of additional therapeutic targets, and biomarker-guided strategies to overcome αPD-1 resistance. Accordingly, a clinical trial evaluating sequential axatilimab, PTX, and retifanlimab has been initiated (NCT06320405).
